strengths: The paper targets a relevant and underexplored setting: joint video super-resolution and deblurring under dynamically varying exposure, which is well motivated by auto-exposure and low-light capture behavior in real videos.

The proposed framework is technically coherent: HRBP provides parallel sequence-level temporal propagation, ETM injects exposure-conditioned features, and exposure-aware FGDF extends the prior FMA-Net degradation modeling in a plausible way.

Experimental results are strong across the proposed REDS-ME/REDS-RE benchmarks and GoPro, with consistent gains over retrained baselines including FMA-Net, BSSTNet, RVRT, IART, BasicVSR++, and Ev-DeblurVSR. The reported efficiency is also attractive relative to several competitive baselines.

The paper includes useful ablations for temporal modeling strategy, exposure guidance, number of HRBP blocks, degradation-aware attention, multi-flow hypotheses, FGDF vs conventional dynamic filtering, and loss components. These ablations mostly support the claimed design choices.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with implementation details, training stages, dataset construction, supplementary analyses, and limitations described in reasonable detail.
weaknesses: The central real-world claim remains only partially validated. The new benchmarks are synthetic and derived from REDS using frame interpolation, averaging, and bicubic downsampling; they do not model sensor noise, nonlinear camera response, rolling shutter, ISP effects, or spatially varying illumination/exposure, all of which matter for real exposure changes.

The exposure-aware gains from ETE are modest on the main in-distribution REDS-ME setting, e.g. about 0.1 dB on REDS4-ME-5:4/5:5. Larger gains appear on REDS-RE and GoPro, but the evidence does not fully isolate whether this comes from exposure modeling rather than extra capacity, pretraining, or dataset-specific correlations.

The method is quite complex, combining a pretrained ETE, NetD, NetR, HRBP, multi-flow-mask prediction, DA attention, RAFT supervision, and a three-stage training procedure. The incremental novelty over FMA-Net is meaningful but somewhat architectural and engineering-heavy rather than conceptually simple.

The benchmark construction may favor the proposed method because the exposure labels used for ETE pretraining match the synthetic exposure levels used in REDS-ME/REDS-RE. More evidence on continuously varying real captures with ground truth, or at least stronger real-video evaluation, would make the claims more convincing.

Reproducibility depends on details not fully evidenced in the main text, such as exact retraining protocols for all baselines, runtime measurement conditions, release plans for REDS-ME/REDS-RE, and whether code/model weights will be made available.

The limitations section is honest but also highlights important remaining gaps: dependence on 2D optical flow can fail under complex 3D/non-rigid motion, and the synthetic degradation model omits several coupled real camera effects. These gaps temper the breadth of the real-world claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer vision problem: joint video super-resolution and deblurring under changing exposure, which is a plausible real-world failure mode for existing VSR/VSRDB systems.

The proposed FMA-Net++ system is technically coherent and combines several reasonable ingredients: hierarchical bidirectional propagation, exposure-conditioned modulation, degradation-aware attention, and flow-guided dynamic filtering.

The experimental section is broad, with comparisons against SR, deblurring, VSR, blind VSR, and joint VSRDB baselines. The paper also includes ablations for temporal modeling, ETE guidance, number of flow-mask pairs, filtering design, and losses.
The supplementary material provides useful implementation details, training schedules, dataset construction procedures, and limitations, which improves reproducibility relative to many submissions.
The method reports consistent improvements over retrained FMA-Net and other baselines on the proposed REDS-ME/RE benchmarks and on GoPro, with favorable parameter/runtime numbers.
weaknesses: The core contribution appears incremental over FMA-Net rather than a clearly new algorithmic advance. Many components are inherited or adapted from prior work: FGDF from FMA-Net, SFT-style exposure modulation, Restormer-style attention blocks, RAFT supervision, and standard synthetic blur generation. The paper presents the combination confidently, but the conceptual novelty is modest.

The central claim of handling unknown dynamically varying exposure is not fully convincing. The exposure-aware feature extractor is trained with discrete synthetic exposure labels from five constructed levels, and the benchmarks largely follow the same synthetic process. This does not establish robust handling of real, continuous, camera-dependent auto-exposure dynamics.

The new benchmarks are useful but limited. REDS-ME and REDS-RE are derived from REDS using frame interpolation and averaging, then bicubic downsampling. This synthetic pipeline may not capture sensor noise, nonlinear camera response, rolling shutter, ISP effects, saturation, or illumination changes coupled with exposure. As a result, strong performance on these benchmarks may overstate real-world applicability.

The real-world evidence is weak. Real smartphone videos are shown qualitatively with no ground truth, limited acquisition detail, and only no-reference metrics such as NIQE/MUSIQ. These metrics are not enough to substantiate the strong claims of real-world generalization.

The ablation evidence does not fully isolate the proposed ideas. For example, ETE adds parameters and gives only small gains on REDS4-ME, while the larger gains on REDS-RE/GoPro may reflect the synthetic training setup or extra capacity rather than a well-validated exposure representation. The paper does not compare against simpler alternatives such as blur-severity embeddings, exposure-ratio regression, blind degradation tokens, or matched-parameter variants.

The efficiency claims require more careful treatment. Runtime is reported per LR frame, but the sequence-level parallel architecture may have different latency, memory, and streaming behavior from recurrent methods. The paper does not adequately analyze full-sequence latency, peak memory, batching, or deployment constraints.

The paper repeatedly describes the degradation kernels as physically grounded, but the actual formulation is a learned approximation trained on synthetic averaging and pseudo-flow supervision. The physical derivation is mostly motivational and does not validate that the learned kernels correspond to real exposure-motion integration.

Several comparisons may be unfair or incomplete. Some baselines are retrained, others are cascaded or adapted, and the degree of tuning for each is unclear. The event-based baseline is included despite requiring different inputs, but the discussion does not fully clarify what conclusions should or should not be drawn from that comparison.

The paper would benefit from stronger failure analysis. The limitations mention synthetic data and 2D flow, but there are few concrete failure cases, no robustness analysis under noise/ISP changes/incorrect exposure statistics, and no evaluation on captured dynamic-exposure data with controlled settings.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored setting for joint video super-resolution and deblurring: dynamically varying exposure coupled with motion blur. This is well motivated by real camera auto-exposure behavior and is a meaningful extension beyond fixed-exposure VSRDB assumptions.

The proposed FMA-Net++ framework is technically coherent. The hierarchical refinement with bidirectional propagation gives a plausible sequence-level alternative to sliding-window and recurrent designs, while ETM and exposure-aware FGDF are well aligned with the stated degradation model.

The experimental evidence is strong overall. The method is compared against a broad set of relevant SR, deblurring, VSR, video deblurring, blind VSR, and joint VSRDB baselines, with retraining on the proposed data where appropriate. Gains over strong baselines such as FMA-Net*, BSSTNet*, and RVRT* are consistent on REDS4-ME, REDS-RE, and GoPro.

The ablations are useful and cover the main claims: temporal modeling strategy, ETE guidance, number of HRBP blocks, degradation-aware attention, multi-flow-mask pairs, exposure-aware FGDF, and loss terms. These studies make the contribution more convincing than a pure benchmark-gain paper.

The paper includes new evaluation resources, REDS-ME and REDS-RE, designed specifically for multi-exposure and random-exposure VSRDB. Even though synthetic, they provide a systematic way to evaluate an issue that current benchmarks do not isolate well.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with a detailed supplement including implementation settings, dataset generation, additional qualitative results, and limitations.
weaknesses: The central evidence still relies heavily on synthetically generated exposure variation from REDS using interpolation, averaging, and downsampling. The authors acknowledge this limitation, but real sensor response, noise, rolling shutter, ISP effects, and spatially varying lighting are not modeled, so the strength of the real-world claim is somewhat limited.

The real-world evaluation is qualitative plus no-reference metrics such as NIQE and MUSIQ. These are helpful but not definitive for restoration quality, and there is no user study or real paired/controlled capture benchmark to validate the dynamic-exposure claim under actual camera pipelines.

Some performance gains from the exposure-aware ETE are modest on in-distribution REDS4-ME, e.g. around 0.1 dB, with larger gains mainly on REDS-RE and GoPro. The paper would be stronger with variance or repeated runs to show that smaller margins are robust.

The method has several moving parts: ETE pretraining, HRBP, multi-flow hypotheses, DA attention, exposure-aware FGDF, staged training, and RAFT supervision. While ablated, the overall system complexity is substantial, and the paper could better discuss which components are essential for practical adoption versus incremental refinements.

The benchmark construction uses discrete exposure ratios and then REDS-RE random walks over those discrete levels. This approximates auto-exposure but may not capture continuous exposure changes, exposure gain interactions, or low-light noise, which are important in the real scenarios motivating the work.

The paper claims physically grounded degradation modeling, but the learned kernel formulation is still an approximation supervised through reconstruction and pseudo-flow. More direct validation of estimated kernels or exposure representations against physical measurements would make this claim stronger.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important setting: joint video super-resolution and deblurring under frame-wise exposure-duration variation. This is a meaningful extension beyond fixed-exposure VSRDB assumptions and is well connected to real camera behavior such as auto-exposure.

The proposed FMA-Net++ combines several coherent design choices: hierarchical bidirectional temporal aggregation for sequence-level parallelism, exposure-time-aware modulation, and exposure-aware flow-guided dynamic filtering. The architecture is technically plausible and the degradation/restoration decoupling is clearly explained.

The experimental section is strong overall. The paper compares against a broad set of relevant SR, deblurring, VSR, blind VSR, and joint VSRDB baselines, including retrained variants where appropriate. Reported gains are consistent across REDS4-ME, REDS-RE, and GoPro, with especially large gains over FMA-Net on dynamic exposure and GoPro.

Efficiency is a real strength. FMA-Net++ reports better accuracy while being substantially faster than several strong baselines, and the paper provides parameter/runtime comparisons rather than focusing only on PSNR/SSIM.

The ablations are useful and relatively thorough: temporal modeling variants, ETE removal and capacity matching, alternative exposure-conditioning designs, corrupted guidance, fixed-input sensitivity, HRBA depth, attention design, number of flow-mask pairs, FGDF variants, and loss coefficients. These support the main architectural claims better than a single component ablation would.

The new REDS-ME and REDS-RE benchmarks are a useful contribution for controlled evaluation of exposure-dependent blur, and the supplement provides reasonably detailed synthesis and implementation protocols. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges unmodeled camera factors such as gain, white balance, clipping, dynamic range, and sensor noise.
weaknesses: The paper’s strongest evidence is on synthetic benchmarks derived from REDS using interpolation and controlled exposure simulation. Although GoPro and real-world qualitative examples help, the real-world validation remains limited: smartphone results use no-reference metrics and visual crops, without user studies, real paired data, or more systematic real-video evaluation. This weakens the claim of strong real-world generalization.

The exposure modeling is tied to discrete synthetic exposure levels used as pseudo-labels for ETE pretraining. The paper argues that the learned embedding interpolates, but this is only indirectly supported. More evaluation on continuous or unseen exposure ratios would make the exposure-awareness claim more convincing.

Novelty is moderate rather than exceptional. HRBA, attention-based temporal aggregation, feature modulation, dynamic filtering, RAFT pseudo-supervision, and synthetic blur generation all build on established components. The paper’s value comes from integration and empirical performance, but some parts read as an incremental extension of FMA-Net rather than a fundamentally new restoration paradigm.

The benchmark construction deliberately omits several camera effects that often covary with exposure in real videos, including gain/noise, saturation/clipping, rolling shutter, tone mapping, and white balance shifts. This is acknowledged, but it means the proposed REDS-ME/RE benchmarks may only partially capture the real degradation distribution claimed in the motivation.

Some fairness questions remain in the comparisons. The paper states that relevant baselines are retrained on REDS-ME, but details about matching training budgets, sequence lengths, data augmentations, optimization schedules, and architecture-specific tuning are not fully visible in the main paper. Since FMA-Net++ is carefully tailored to the new benchmark, stronger reproducibility and baseline-training details are important.

The method appears relatively complex, with three-stage training, frozen contrastive exposure features, degradation prior prediction, RAFT pseudo-flow supervision, multi-flow-mask pairs, and separate NetD/NetR modules. The practical burden is mitigated by fast inference, but training complexity and sensitivity to synthetic data generation deserve more discussion.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored setting: joint video super-resolution and deblurring under frame-wise exposure-duration variation. This is a plausible practical issue for handheld video, and the attempt to isolate it via REDS-ME and REDS-RE is useful.

The experimental section is fairly broad: it compares against SR, deblurring, VSR, blind VSR, and joint VSRDB baselines, includes retrained variants, reports temporal consistency and runtime, and provides ablations for HRBA, ETE/ETM, conditioning alternatives, guidance corruption, multi-flow pairs, and losses.

The proposed model appears computationally attractive relative to several strong video restoration baselines, with favorable reported accuracy/runtime tradeoffs and lower memory than VRT in the stated setting.

The authors acknowledge an important limitation: the synthetic benchmarks isolate blur extent from exposure duration and do not model ISO/gain, white balance, clipping, dynamic range, sensor noise, or spatially varying illumination.
weaknesses: The central contribution is quite incremental. Much of the system is an assembly or extension of existing ingredients: FMA-Net-style flow-guided dynamic filtering and degradation/restoration decoupling, SFT-like modulation, Restormer attention/FFN modules, RAFT pseudo-supervision, and a ResNet-18 contrastive exposure encoder. The paper does not convincingly establish that the conceptual advance goes much beyond a carefully engineered FMA-Net variant.

The benchmark evidence is heavily synthetic and potentially circular. REDS-ME/RE are generated from REDS by averaging interpolated high-frame-rate sequences into five discrete exposure levels, and those same discrete exposure levels become pseudo-labels for ETE pretraining. This makes it unclear how much of the reported exposure-awareness transfers to real camera exposure changes, where gain/noise/clipping/rolling shutter/tone mapping may covary with exposure.

Real-world validation is weak for the strength of the claims. The paper relies on selected qualitative examples and no-reference NIQE/MUSIQ scores, which are not reliable enough to support strong claims of real-world generalization. There is no real captured dataset with ground truth, controlled exposure metadata, user study, or robust blind perceptual evaluation.

The claimed exposure-aware mechanism is not fully disentangled from model capacity and benchmark construction. Table 4 shows that a capacity-matched model without ETE nearly matches or slightly exceeds FMA-Net++ on fixed REDS-ME-5:4 PSNR and is close on REDS-ME-5:5; the larger gains appear mainly on REDS-RE, which is exactly the synthetic split constructed from the same discrete exposure anchors used for ETE supervision.

The method assumes that exposure can be inferred from the degraded RGB frames alone, but this is ill-posed: motion magnitude, texture content, scene depth, lighting, and exposure duration can produce similar blur appearances. The paper does not adequately analyze failure cases or ambiguity in exposure estimation beyond a synthetic kNN confusion matrix.

The dataset construction depends on video frame interpolation to 1920 fps before averaging. This may introduce artifacts or overly smooth latent trajectories, and the paper does not quantify how interpolation errors affect training/evaluation or whether methods exploit artifacts specific to the synthesis pipeline.

The comparison protocol leaves some fairness and reproducibility questions. It states that relevant SOTA methods were adapted and retrained, but details of adaptation, training budgets, tuning effort, event-method handling, and whether all methods receive equally favorable settings are not sufficiently transparent in the main paper.

The writing repeatedly overstates conclusions. Phrases such as strong out-of-distribution performance and robust real-world generalization are not fully justified by the available evidence, especially given that GoPro is still a synthetic/controlled deblurring benchmark rather than a direct test of dynamic auto-exposure in standard RGB videos.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and practically important variant of joint video super-resolution and deblurring: frame-wise exposure-duration variation, which is a realistic failure mode for fixed-exposure restoration models.

The proposed FMA-Net++ combines several coherent design choices: HRBA for sequence-level parallel temporal aggregation, exposure-time-aware modulation, and exposure-aware flow-guided dynamic filtering. The architecture is well aligned with the stated degradation model rather than being a purely empirical add-on.

The experimental evidence is strong overall. The paper compares against many relevant SR, deblurring, VSR, blind VSR, and joint VSRDB baselines, including retrained versions on the proposed data, and reports consistent gains on REDS-ME, REDS-RE, GoPro, and real-world examples.
Efficiency is a meaningful strength: FMA-Net++ is substantially faster than FMA-Net and several transformer/recurrent baselines while improving restoration quality and temporal consistency.

The ablation section is unusually thorough. The authors test temporal modeling variants, capacity-matched no-ETE baselines, alternative exposure-conditioning designs, corrupted exposure guidance, fixed-input sensitivity, number of HRBA blocks, attention choices, multi-flow-mask pairs, and loss terms. These analyses make the main claims more convincing.
The new REDS-ME and REDS-RE benchmarks are useful for controlled evaluation of exposure-dependent blur. The synthesis protocol and limitations are described clearly in the supplementary material.

The paper is generally clear, well organized, and technically detailed, with implementation settings and dataset construction described sufficiently for a reviewer to understand the method and evaluation.
weaknesses: The main benchmark contribution is still synthetic and controlled. REDS-ME/RE model exposure duration through blur extent, but intentionally omit ISO/gain changes, clipping, noise, white balance, dynamic range changes, and spatially varying illumination. This limits how strongly the results support real camera robustness claims.

Real-world validation is qualitative plus no-reference metrics only. The examples are encouraging, but the paper would be stronger with a larger real-world evaluation, user study, or a more systematic assessment of temporal artifacts under actual auto-exposure changes.

The exposure-aware component appears most beneficial on REDS-RE and GoPro, but on fixed-exposure REDS-ME the capacity-matched no-ETE model nearly closes the PSNR gap. This somewhat narrows the evidence for exposure modeling to dynamic/generalization settings, where the benchmarks are still synthetic or indirect.

The method depends on exposure pseudo-labels from the synthetic construction for ETE pretraining. It is not fully clear how robust the exposure embedding would be under real exposure metadata distributions, different frame rates, nonlinear camera pipelines, or scenes where motion blur and texture statistics confound exposure estimation.

The novelty is solid but partly incremental: HRBA, dynamic filtering, optical-flow-guided restoration, Restormer-style attention components, and contrastive embeddings are individually familiar. The contribution is mainly their effective integration for variable-exposure VSRDB rather than a fundamentally new restoration paradigm.

Reproducibility would benefit from an explicit commitment to release code, trained models, and the generated REDS-ME/RE splits. The paper gives many implementation details, but the review version does not make artifact availability fully clear.
